Text: How many hours do you need to exercise to lose weight? That depends on how much weight you're trying to lose, and what your diet looks like. If you eat a lot of unhealthy food, and/or simply eat too much food, then lots of exercise might be needed just to maintain. If you eat a fairly healthy diet and watch your calorie intake, then it might not take all that much exercise to lose weight. Of course, I'm not a health professional, so you might want the advice of a doctor, dietician, etc. In general, as far as a weight-loss program, I tend to see at least two basic approaches. And, just to be clear, I'm not advocating for either, here. I've just observed that these are the two most talked about: The first approach is to focus on calories. You need to burn more calories than you take in. If you're eating a lot of calories, then you need to either exercise more, or eat less. Or both. The second is to focus on macros and the types of foods you eat, like keto, paleo, etc. Some of these approaches focus on burning fat, rather than focusing on calories. Again, I'm not saying that one approach is better than the other. Both approaches have had their fair share of success stories and horror stories. But, I would say it's very difficult to lose weight and keep it off without both a calorie and a macro focus. And I'm not saying a calorie-focused or macro-focused approach *has to* be difficult, either. But it is a long-term lifestyle change, not a quick fix. And there’s plenty of misleading marketing, which can make the whole process extra difficult. For example, there are tons of weight loss supplements on the market with limited scientific backing. Many of these supplements prey on the desire for a quick fix. Just, stick to the basics: eat a healthy diet, exercise regularly, and make gradual changes. Don't make any drastic changes, and you'll be able to stick to it longer.

Text: Do they still teach the myth about Columbus being the first European to reach the Americas in US schools? They don't teach that myth, but some schools might still teach other myths. One that still persists, even though it has been rejected by almost all serious researchers and historians, is the very idea of 'great men' in history. You know, like the 'great man' who 'invented' the lightbulb, the 'great man' that discovered gravity, and maybe one of the biggest myths out there, the 'great man' hero who supposedly invented the internet. It's very convenient that all of these 'great men' were white. I remember being taught this in my high school history classes, and it seemed like pretty much everyone was white, European, male, and the possessor of some divine insight. In reality, the lightbulb and internet, for example, were not just the idea of one person. The lightbulb went through decades of research, experiments, and improvements by various people, with the 'great man' just being the one who was the final popularizer. Likewise, the internet wasn't just 'invented' by one person. It was the result of a whole series of innovations that, over several decades, grew and expanded. Many of these 'great men' also didn’t accomplish particular achievements, on their own, at their own initiative. They were instead a product of the times, as well as benefitting from the work of other people, and most of the time were only getting ahead. However, the great man theory is an easy idea to sell. It's a simple narrative, in which a single person can be credited for all the good things that happened. It also conveniently aligns with a narrative that puts white men on top as the ones who deserve all the accolades. It's been rejected, by historians, as a simplification of reality, and as a vehicle for the glorification of certain people at the expense of others. But it still persists, especially in popular culture, which is, of course, where most people get a lot of their 'history' from.

Text: Why do people seem to think gun control laws matter when in reality if I want to obtain a gun and the government thought it could stop me, I'd just obtain a gun through illegal means? Well, it's not that simple. I think people often underestimate the real effect of gun control, even if they're right that it can't absolutely stop every bad actor from obtaining a firearm. The truth is, we don't know what the exact effect of any gun control law will be. It only makes intellectual sense to assume that reducing the overall number of guns available to the public will reduce gun violence. The question mark is how and by how much. Consider the many different types of gun violence that exist. Some, like mass shootings, are relatively rare, but they get the most media coverage, and thus the most legislative attention. Other types of gun violence, like suicides, are far more common, and the type of gun control law that might prevent it will be different. Still, there is also no question that a lot of the gun violence is due to the illicit availability of firearms used in crimes. No one would dispute the idea that any gun control law aimed at this type of firearm should have a real impact, by further restricting their availability. After all, that's why you have these laws in the first place, even if they're not always a complete success. It's a little like how we try to prevent illegal drugs from entering the US. No one thinks we'll be able to stop every drug that comes across the border but it keeps some percentage of them out. A sensible approach would be to implement a set of gun laws to prevent different types of access, tailored to the types of problems those gun control laws would be addressing, such as by restricting certain types of firearms. And, like any science, you need to keep gathering evidence and rethinking the approach to make it work better.

Text: So why are pilots who have been flying for years all saying they know the earth is flat? They’re not. Not only does this run contrary to a massive body of evidence, but it’s not even what pilots themselves say. Pilots use a lot of scientific principles as part of their job, and understand basic physics. Even the curvature of the Earth is taken into account when charting a flight path. You can't just go from Point A to Point B in a straight line if the Earth is a sphere, particularly when traveling over longer distances. And yet, there are people who *claim* that pilots are saying that the Earth is flat, and thus should be trusted. But why would anyone trust the claims of people who are demonstrably wrong about what pilots are saying? As I said before, without evidence-based reasoning, methods are worthless at this task. The reality is that a very, very small percentage of pilots, if any, actually believe the Earth is flat. You can easily find instances of people claiming to be such, but their claims are easily debunked when they try to explain their "evidence”. I mean, a brief web search for "pilot flat earth" comes up with nothing but debunking videos and articles. So in the meantime, it's best to disregard such claims, regardless of how they are presented.

Text: Maybe a biology teach in a public school can’t teach the truth about the existence of life. But can she point out the fallacies of evolution without speaking about creationism? Is that unconstitutional? I'm not a legal scholar, but I'm guessing the answer is 'no'. As long as the teacher isn't advocating for a particular religious viewpoint, she should be able to offer a truly balanced perspective on the subject. If she's merely pointing out the areas where the theory of evolution has some gaps and unanswered questions, she could be teaching perfectly acceptable science. Now, you've got to be careful here. There's a fine line between that and promoting a specific religious agenda. For example, I don't think it's appropriate for our biology teacher to say something like, "Well, the science just isn't there yet for how everything got started, but that's because God did it." That's obviously promoting a certain religious viewpoint. But she might be able to say something like, "While we know the basic framework of how species evolve over time, we still have some open questions about the origin of life and the conditions that allowed it to begin." That's just stating scientific fact, and it's still appropriate. It would go without saying that she shouldn’t give any undue weight to creationist arguments. In the same way that science courses shouldn't give any undue weight to astrology. It's pretty clear that creationism doesn't meet the standards of science. But in the interests of thoroughness, she may even be able to briefly mention creationism, but only to illustrate why it's not a legitimate scientific theory. It's tough to say exactly where the line is. But there's a wide range of possible scenarios, and it seems like many of them would be perfectly fine.

Text: Could Kamala Harris beat Donald Trump? That’s a tough one. I could go back and forth, running through the various arguments. Depending on the day, you can find arguments for either side. For example, one of the biggest arguments that Donald Trump could lose is the sheer unpopularity of the man himself, or rather, of his political positions. He really does have a lot of baggage that’s hard, maybe even impossible, for him to shake off. Of course, there are plenty of arguments against Kamala Harris. For example, the economy, the crime rate, and a whole host of other issues that are currently going on could sink her. And any one particular event could swing the election one way or the other. The 2024 election is going to see a lot of mudslinging, and I don’t think it will be very pleasant to watch. No one knows for sure how the election will play out, but it will be very close. Just like in 2020, the election probably will depend on the swing states, and it could be a very long night before we know the final results. Of course, you do have plenty of other candidates running for president, too. Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. and Marianne Williamson are two of the most prominent third-party candidates seeking the presidency. But neither is likely to be elected. They might make things more difficult for the two main candidates, but that’s about it. And that’s not even taking into account any potential third-party candidates in the future either. So honestly, I don’t know who would win the election. But one thing’s for sure: it will be highly contested and will be sure to be quite a spectacle.

Text: Scientists dabble and meddle in the genome with the intent to make life better, but are they really, intentionally or unintentionally, redefining or redesigning life? If so, how? That’s a significant question, and it gets even more philosophically complicated when you consider what “better” actually means. For example, scientists can manipulate genes, and often do, to give a particular breed of, say, dog, specific traits. Often, this is to fulfill the desires of pet owners. So, is that making life better? For those owners, perhaps. For the dog? Maybe. But it could be that in the long run, the dog’s genetic modifications lead to a shorter lifespan than it otherwise might have. SOURCE: The Genetics of Dog Breeding | VCA Animal Hospitals That’s more often the case than not, since there's a reason why most dog breeds are unhealthy: there are too few members of their species to maintain the population’s health. Humans have intervened with the dog’s genome, through selective breeding, to give them more human-centric qualities at the cost of their biological health. Consider how you want a dog to behave in your house, as opposed to how likely that dog is to live a long, healthy life. One of those will win out over the other. In fact, there's a great argument to be made that dogs would be much better off in an evolutionary sense if humans were not involved in their evolutionary development at all. Just a random thought of mine. As for the question of redefining or redesigning life, the answer is a definitive yes. Scientists are doing both, and even if they weren't intentionally, they’re making the same impact. For all the advancements we've made, there are still countless questions to be answered about the very concept of life.

Text: Is music at best better than food? That's an interesting question. I'd have to say it depends on the music and the food. It's like asking if a good book is better than a good movie. Both can be enjoyable, and both are completely different experiences. If you're starving, food has a clear advantage. You need food to live, and the best music isn't going to help with that. But if you're not hungry, a really moving piece of music can be a more profound experience than a meal, no matter how good the meal is. Think of a specific concert, or a live performance. The experience is communal, and something that you can’t get just listening to a recording later. Of course, it depends on the type of music you listen to. Somebody who listens to nothing but polka music could have a different opinion than somebody who’s into classical. A country fan might disagree with a heavy metal fan. And different people will react to different genres or musical styles differently. There's also the issue of time. You can listen to a piece of music over and over. You can certainly eat a delicious meal over and over, but each meal is a unique experience that is gone forever. It’s harder to replicate the pleasure of a really fulfilling musical experience again and again. So, in the end, both food and music have their own strengths and weaknesses. They both serve different purposes, and elicit different emotions. Ultimately, it comes down to personal preference.

This is a straightforward physics problem, making it quite unlike many other questions people ask. And by all means, physics problems aren't hard. You just need to understand the concepts. Here's the important concept to understand: The buoyant force is equal to the weight of the liquid displaced. In this case, the buoyant force is 8N. You can also think of the buoyant force as the amount by which the object appears to weigh less in water as opposed to in air. So, the weight of the object in water is 12N, but in air, the object weighs more. Now, what's the difference between an object's weight in air and its weight in water? It's the buoyant force. If the weight of the object in water is 12N, and the buoyant force is 8N, what is the weight of the object in air? Simple subtraction will do the trick: you just add the buoyant force to the weight of the object in water (12N + 8N = 20N). Therefore, the object weighs 20N in air. Pretty simple, eh? You'd think it'd be more complicated, but that's the elegance of physics: even when issues *are* complex, the relationships between forces and interactions are often relatively simple.

Text: Is it better to fly two long haul flights (say 10 hours each) instead of one ultra-long haul flight (about 18-19 hours)? It depends on the context. If you're mainly concerned about getting from Point A to Point B as quickly as possible, then you'd lean towards the ultra-long haul flight. You'd spend a little less time in transit. But then you have to consider everything else that goes along with that. Those ultra-long haul flights can be rough. You're squished into a chair for nearly a full day, dealing with the same recirculated air and the same noisy strangers. And if you're used to getting up and stretching your legs, you're not going to have as many opportunities to do that. You can try to take advantage of the airplane’s bathroom, but the aisles are usually pretty cramped, and it’s still not the same as walking around on solid ground. Plus, you’d be subjected to the same in-flight entertainment for the whole flight. So many movies and TV shows, no matter how good they are, can get repetitive after a while. There’s also the issue of flight delays. If one of the flights is delayed, there's no guarantee that the second flight will accommodate the change. So you'd be standing at the airport for a long time, probably without any good food or comfortable seating. On the other hand, two shorter flights can offer more flexibility. You have the possibility of better in-flight entertainment; you have a better chance of stretching your legs, and changing the ambient air. You also get to experience two different airports and the novelty of dealing with the airport staff twice and navigating two very different environments. So while an ultra-long haul flight might seem better in theory, the reality is more nuanced. If you're really worried about the duration of the journey, consider the impact on your well-being and whether or not the added time in transit balances with an overall better experience.

Text: You say that Darwin proved we are all animals, but animals rarely practice birthcontrol, then why you do? The premise of the question is a bit off, I think. Darwin didn’t set out to ‘prove’ that we are all animals. That was one of the logical conclusions of his theories, but the goal of *On the Origin of Species* was figuring out the mechanics of evolution. And to answer your question, the practice of birth control isn't that complex. Humans take advantage of their higher level of intelligence, and their ability to modify their environment, to change their breeding patterns. So many different animals are able to exercise some level of control over their breeding habits. For example, in captivity, there is artificial insemination, and selective breeding based on desired traits. In the wild, various animals will leave their territories, or even kill their young to avoid overpopulation. But the real point I’d make is that these are minor modifications on top of a bigger point: birth control isn't always necessary. Plenty of animals don't have a very big percentage of fertile offspring, or suffer high infant mortality. And for those types of animals, or in those environments, there’s little evolutionary pressure to invent birth control. Also, it’s worth asking: what does ‘control’ mean? Humans can use birth control to have no kids. But humans also want to have kids, and they want to maximize their chances of having kids. Human beings have the ability to ‘control’ when it is best to have children.

Text: As a native-English-language-speaker, is there ever situation in which you actually should not speak perfectly accurate English as defined by most academically approved English grammar and vocabulary books? Absolutely. First off, let’s clarify what we mean by ‘perfectly accurate English.’ Are we talking about proper grammar, spelling, and lexicon as taught in school, or something more? If it's the former, then no, it’s not always necessary, or even desirable.  There are a whole host of situations where less-than-perfect grammar and usage are appropriate. A few examples of these situations are:  *   **Context:** If speaking to small children, or people learning English, you often have to simplify your language. You wouldn't want to give an advanced lecture to a toddler. *   **Dialect, Slang, & Other Idioms:** If you’re trying to fit into a specific culture, then using colloquial English or even another language entirely is the best way to be understood and accepted. Similarly, various subcultures might involve specialized vocabulary, so you might need to do the same. *   **Artistic Expression:** Creative writing, acting, music, etc., frequently involve deliberately breaking grammatical rules to create certain effects. Punctuation too. Think about the use of stream-of-consciousness in novels, or certain musical choices that deliberately stray from the norm. *   **Communicating Effectively:** Sometimes, the best way to communicate is a little vague. As an example, sarcasm and humor can require breaking of the rules.  Of course, I'm not advocating for the abandonment of proper English. It’s still critically important for clear communication and to be understood by the widest possible audience. But, if you are trying to be understood by a much smaller audience then the rules are there simply to inform you of what to do. They are not commands. And it’s not enough to just know the rules, you also have to know when to break them.

Text: Some worry that the United States is in an unusually anti-intellectual period right now. Is this really the case? Haven't societies always been composed mostly of people who are rather unthinking and just want "bread and circuses"? I think there's some truth to that. I’m not sure if America's in the worst shape it's ever been, but even if it isn’t, it's not exactly in terrific shape either. It's also certainly true that every civilization through history has had a sizable portion of people who aren't overly concerned with intellectual pursuits. And to be clear, I don’t mean every single person has to be a rocket scientist or read Plato in the original Greek. We all have lives to live, and there are plenty of valid reasons for not spending a lot of time on intellectual endeavors. But when a sizable percentage of the population is actively hostile to intellectualism, that's a different story. And that’s exactly the kind of problem that societies have faced throughout human history. As far back as the ancient Greeks, philosophers and scientists had to deal with an anti-intellectual sentiment that was already well-established. This wasn't even an exclusively problem in any particular democracy vs. oligarchy or whatever governmental system either. Even some of history's most enlightened leaders had to deal with the problem. But those were simpler times. Today, we have the Internet and easily accessed misinformation and disinformation campaigns run by foreign/domestic bad actors with a goal in mind. And there are plenty of folks out there who are just eating up the lies.

Text: Are atheists truly correct if everything has to have a creator? The Earth can't come out of nothingness. It had to be created by something. If everything has to have a creator, then who created that creator? This is a question that's been asked by both believers and non-believers for ages. But even assuming some kind of intelligent design, who designed the designer? What made it create? There's no obvious place to just stop and say 'that's just the way things are' any more than there's a stopping point for explaining how the universe got started. It's a regress, and that's the central issue with the argument from design. However, there are arguments supporting that everything can come from nothing in areas of physics like quantum mechanics. A common one is that the universe is not static. It is constantly expanding, so something, like energy, is being created from nothing, just every second of every day. But that, too, is not a perfect answer. We can observe something that happened, but can't really understand how things are happening at the most fundamental level. Nonetheless, it doesn't really make sense to simply state that there is a creator, the creator just "is" and always was - because that's not much more helpful than saying everything just appeared one day, with no particular rhyme or reason. And, as it turns out, a God concept raises further questions. After all, what are the physical characteristics of this God? What is its mind like? Does it have any goals or desires? As a result, it tends to add complexity to the situation rather than eliminate it.

Text: Have you ever met an intelligent creationist? I used to have a great, and indeed, frequent, neighbor who was as devout in his faith as I was in my engineering work. We had many friendly debates about religion, and honestly, he was one of the smartest, most well-read people I’ve ever known. He could cite scripture and philosophy and science and history like nobody’s business, and he had an exceptional ability to make his arguments very clear. And that's the rub, in the end. Clarity doesn't make an argument right. Even he would admit that his particular interpretation of scripture had some shortcomings. But for the life of me, I can't remember him ever making truly compelling arguments in favor of actual, literal, young-Earth creationism. Perhaps he just didn't want to alienate me, but I never heard him make those kinds of arguments. The reason why is because, well, those arguments don't stand up to science. And if someone truly understands how science works, they're going to understand that, and they're going to be hesitant to argue against it. And as I mentioned before, science is the best tool we humans have for understanding objective issues. You can define "intelligent" any way you like, and certainly some people could probably fit the definition given some parameters. But in the end, it really depends on what parameters you use.
